analysis.one_liner: Bans no-knock warrants for federal agents and DOJ-funded state and local police.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the House on December 10, 2025 with 31 cosponsors and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which has taken no further action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill says federal law enforcement officers must announce their authority and purpose before breaking into a home with a warrant, ending no-knock entries at the federal level. State and local police departments that receive Justice Department money would be required to do the same. It is named for Breonna Taylor, who was killed in her Louisville apartment during a 2020 no-knock raid.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose homes are raided by police — most often in drug investigations, and disproportionately in Black and low-income neighborhoods. The bill requires officers to knock and announce themselves before forcing entry, which lowers the chance of someone being shot while they mistake police for an intruder.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of homes targeted in police raids

how_it_helps.text: Federal officers could not execute a warrant until after providing notice of their authority and purpose, prohibiting federal no-knock entries [S2] [S3].
State and local agencies that receive Department of Justice funds could not execute warrants that do not require notice before forcibly entering a premises [S2] [S3].
The bill uses federal grant money as the lever, so departments that want DOJ funding must adopt a knock-and-announce requirement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal and DOJ-funded local police agencies lose the option of unannounced entry. Departments would have to change how they serve warrants, and lose the tactical surprise that officers argue protects them in some drug raids.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal and DOJ-funded local police agencies

drawbacks.text: Officers' groups and some prosecutors argue that announcing before entry gives suspects time to arm themselves or destroy evidence, which can make warrant service more dangerous for officers and neighbors [S3] (the bill eliminates unannounced entries without a case-by-case exception).
The bill contains no exception for situations where knocking would create immediate danger, such as hostage or barricade scenarios, which opponents could cite in arguing for a narrower rule [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: knocking gives residents a fair chance to recognize police, but it also takes away an option officers use in high-risk raids. The bill is a clean, narrow rule rather than a nuanced one, so the honest case against it is that some dangerous situations call for exceptions it does not provide. The stakes on the public side are life and death, and the cost side is a policing tactic, not a financial burden on taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has been sitting without a hearing or vote since December 2025; Congress is still in session, so it is not yet dead.

narrative.text: Rep. Morgan McGarvey of Kentucky introduced the bill on December 10, 2025 [S1] [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee, its only action so far [S5].
Thirty-one House members cosponsored it — 30 Democrats and 1 Republican (Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky) [S4].
The Judiciary Committee has taken no further action: no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to change anything: federal and DOJ-funded local police agencies retain their current authority to seek and execute no-knock warrants, and the bill's prospects rest on a committee that has not acted on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies keep no-knock authority for now

for.name: Rep. Morgan McGarvey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 31 cosponsors

for.name: Rep. Thomas Massie
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republican to do so

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is overwhelmingly Democratic — 30 of 217 Democrats versus 1 of 223 Republicans — though the bill's lone Republican cosponsor (Massie) shows it can cross party lines; no vote has occurred to test it further.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal and DOJ-funded state and local police)
industries.note: The bill takes away their authority to execute no-knock warrants and conditions DOJ funding on adopting a knock-and-announce rule. Their institutional interest in keeping unannounced entries runs against the bill's safety purpose for residents of raided homes.

analysis.trajectory: With no action since referral in December 2025, the bill faces long odds: most bills referred to the House Judiciary Committee never receive a hearing or vote, and policing-reform measures have had difficulty reaching the floor in this Congress. Its small but bipartisan base of support is not enough on its own to force action; it would need leadership or committee attention to move, which is not currently evident.
